sections.heading: Worshiping the one God who saves
sections.text: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one God, my salvation: I worship you. You are not three gods, and you are not one lonely person wearing different masks. You are the one living God—Father, Son, and Spirit—and you have made yourself known so that sinners like me can come into your kingdom. I praise you for letting me know you, not as an idea to study from a distance, but as the God who has come near to save me.
theological_themes: The one God exists eternally as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
Knowing God is itself a gift of saving grace.
God brings sinners into his kingdom by revealing himself to them.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus names the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together in the one baptismal name, grounding Christian worship of God as triune rather than merely as a general divine power.

Paul blesses the church in terms of the grace of Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Spirit, showing that Christian salvation and communion with God are experienced through the work of all three persons.

sections.heading: Thanking each Person for saving love
sections.text: Father, thank you for loving me before I loved you and for sending your Son to rescue me. Jesus, thank you for loving me enough to take on my humanity, to give your blood for my sin, and to cover my shame with your righteousness. Holy Spirit, thank you for loving me by coming into my heart, giving me life I could never create in myself, and opening my eyes to the beauty and worth of Jesus.
theological_themes: The Father sends the Son in love for the salvation of sinners.
The Son truly becomes human and saves by his blood and righteousness.
The Holy Spirit gives new life and reveals Christ to the believer.

scripture_references.connection: John presents the sending of the Son as the concrete display of the Father’s love, especially in Christ becoming the atoning sacrifice for sin.
The incarnation is central to this section: the eternal Son truly took on human nature, making the prayer’s gratitude for Jesus assuming our nature biblically grounded.

Paul describes the exchange at the heart of salvation: Christ bears sin, and believers receive righteousness in him, matching the prayer’s language of sin being dealt with and unworthiness being covered.
Jesus says the Spirit will glorify him by taking what is his and declaring it to his people, which supports the prayer’s thanks that the Spirit reveals Christ’s glory.

sections.heading: Praising grace that holds me in Christ
sections.text: Triune God, I bless you for love I did not earn and could never explain. It is strong enough to save the lost and bring them all the way home to glory. Father, thank you for giving me to Jesus and making me his own—his sheep, his treasure, his belonging. Jesus, thank you for receiving me, binding me to yourself, and loving me with a faithful covenant love. Holy Spirit, thank you for showing me Jesus as my salvation, giving me faith, breaking the resistance of my stubborn heart, and joining me to Christ forever.
theological_themes: Salvation is unearned grace from beginning to end.
The Father gives his people to the Son, and the Son keeps them.
The Spirit creates faith, overcomes spiritual resistance, and unites believers to Christ.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus speaks of those given to him by the Father and promises not to cast them out but to raise them up, directly supporting the prayer’s confidence in belonging to Christ by grace.
Jesus describes his people as his sheep, known and kept by him, with the Father’s hand securing them; this closely fits the prayer’s image of being Christ’s sheep and possession.
Faith and salvation are described as God’s gift, not human achievement, which grounds the prayer’s thanks for faith being implanted by grace.
Paul teaches that the believer is joined to the Lord, supporting the prayer’s language of being made one with Christ rather than merely helped by him from a distance.

sections.heading: Relying on you when I pray
sections.text: Father, you are not far away or uninterested; you are seated in authority and you hear me. Jesus, you welcome my prayers and bring me near because of what you have done. Holy Spirit, help me in my weakness. Show me what I truly need. Give shape to prayers I do not know how to speak. Pray within me when I am confused or tired, and strengthen me so I do not give up.
theological_themes: Prayer is offered to the Father through the Son by the help of the Holy Spirit.
Christ’s priestly work gives believers confidence to draw near to God.
The Spirit helps believers pray in weakness and need.

scripture_references.connection: Because Jesus is the great high priest, believers are invited to approach God’s throne with confidence for mercy and help, which supports the prayer’s confidence that Christ receives petitions.
Paul explicitly says the Spirit helps believers in weakness and intercedes when they do not know how to pray, directly grounding this section’s dependence on the Spirit in prayer.
This verse gathers the Trinitarian shape of prayer: access to the Father comes through Christ and in the Spirit, matching the prayer’s movement from Father to Son to Spirit.

sections.heading: Living as someone marked by your name
sections.text: Triune God, you rule over everything, and still you invite me to ask for what matters to your kingdom and to my soul. Teach me to pray for your name to be honored, your kingdom to come, and your will to be done in me and around me. Let my daily life match the name into which I was baptized: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Make me someone who belongs to you openly, trusts you deeply, and seeks your kingdom first.
theological_themes: God’s sovereign rule does not cancel prayer but commands and invites it.
Christian prayer seeks God’s kingdom and the good of the soul.
Baptism into the triune name marks a life of belonging and discipleship.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus teaches his disciples to pray first for God’s name, kingdom, and will, which directly supports asking for things that concern God’s kingdom.
Jesus calls his followers to seek God’s kingdom and righteousness before earthly concerns, matching the prayer’s desire for a life ordered around God’s rule.
The risen Christ commands baptism in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit and ties it to lifelong discipleship, grounding the prayer’s desire to live as one marked by the triune name.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original uses explicit classical Trinitarian language: one Being, one Essence, three distinct Persons. This is historically orthodox Christian doctrine, but it can be difficult to render in contemporary speech without sounding either overly technical or accidentally modalist or tritheist.

The line about the Father having given the believer to Jesus as his sheep, jewel, and portion carries a Reformed/Puritan emphasis on divine election and Christ’s secure possession of his people. Christians from other traditions may nuance that differently, but the adaptation preserves the original’s emphasis.

The language of Jesus having ‘espoused’ the believer reflects biblical covenant and bridal imagery for Christ and his people. In a personal prayer, this can sound strange or overly individualistic, since the New Testament often applies bridal imagery corporately to the church.
significant_interpretive_choices: I rendered ‘assumed my nature’ as Jesus taking on my humanity, to preserve the doctrine of the incarnation without using technical or archaic wording.

I expressed ‘wrought righteousness to cover my unworthiness’ as Jesus covering shame with his righteousness, preserving the substitutionary and justifying sense rather than reducing it to emotional reassurance.
I interpreted ‘implanted faith’ and ‘subdued my stubborn heart’ as the Spirit’s gracious work in regeneration and conversion, not as coercion detached from love.
I kept the concrete images ‘sheep’ and ‘treasure’ from the original’s ‘sheep, jewel, portion,’ while using ‘belonging’ to make ‘portion’ intelligible in contemporary speech.
I treated ‘live and pray as one baptized into the threefold Name’ as a call to whole-life discipleship under the triune name, not merely as a reminder of a past ritual.
